title: The block, sampling, the KV cache

questions.prompt: What does the MLP do that attention doesn't?
options: It lets words exchange information with one another, so each word can pull in context from earlier ones
It works on each word alone: thousands of learned yes/no-style questions whose answers are added to its vector
It turns the final vector into a score for every vocabulary token, ready for softmax to pick from
It stores the keys and values of earlier tokens, so later tokens can look them up without recomputing them
questions.why: A block is talk, then think. Attention is the only place where words see each other; the MLP then works on each word separately with the same weights, which is why it batches so well on a GPU.

questions.prompt: One neuron: inputs x = [1, 1], weights [1, 1], bias −1, then ReLU. What does it output?
questions.why: Dot product 1×1 + 1×1 = 2, plus bias −1 = 1, ReLU keeps positives: max(0, 1) = 1. It fires.

questions.prompt: Same neuron (weights [1, 1], bias −1, ReLU), now x = [1, 0]: only “river earlier” is present. Output?
questions.why: 1×1 + 0×1 = 1, plus bias −1 = 0, max(0, 0) = 0. The bias sets the bar: this neuron fires only when both facts are present.

questions.prompt: In notes = W_down · max(0, W_up · x + b), what do W_up and W_down hold?
options: W_up holds the questions (one row per neuron); W_down holds the note each neuron writes back
W_up holds the vocabulary scores; W_down holds the position of each token in the sequence
W_up is computed fresh for each request from the input x; only W_down is learned in training
Both hold the keys and values cached for earlier tokens, one for keys and one for values
questions.why: Widen, then narrow: W_up asks thousands of questions about the word, ReLU keeps the ones that fire, W_down turns those into notes added to the word's vector. Both are learned weights, frozen at inference.

questions.prompt: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters. Roughly how many of them sit in the MLPs?
options: About 116 billion (roughly two-thirds)
About 17 billion (about 10%)
Exactly 87.5 billion (half)
Almost none: attention holds the weights
questions.why: Per block, attention has about 4 × width² parameters and the MLP about 8 × width², so 8 of 12. In GPT-3 that's about 116 of 175 billion. MLPs are also where factual associations are thought to live.

questions.prompt: What is the residual stream?
options: The leftover probability after top-p cuts the tail, which is spread back over the kept tokens
The word's vector as it passes through the model, each layer's output added to it rather than replacing it
The queue of tokens waiting for decode, each picked up as soon as a batch slot frees up
The error signal flowing backward through every layer during training, which adjusts each layer's weights
questions.why: x = x + attention(x), then x = x + MLP(x), in every block. The final vector is literally the original embedding plus every layer's contribution.

questions.prompt: What would break if each layer replaced the vector instead of adding to it? Pick all that apply.
options: Later layers would lose what earlier layers found unless every layer learned to copy it forward
Training nudges would struggle to reach the early layers
The vocabulary would shrink
The KV cache would no longer be valid
questions.why: Adding keeps everything on a shared notepad and gives gradients a direct path back to early layers. Vocabulary and caching don't depend on it.

questions.prompt: Which backend pattern is the residual stream most like?
options: A cache in front of a database: each layer checks the stream before recomputing a value
An append-only log, or a request context that each middleware enriches rather than replaces
A load balancer that routes each word's vector to whichever layer is least busy
A pipeline where each stage replaces the request object with its own transformed version of it
questions.why: Each layer reads the shared state and adds its contribution, and nothing earlier is discarded. (The KV cache is the one that's like a cache: memoized work.)

questions.prompt: Classic formula: about 12 × width² parameters per block. Width 4,096, 32 blocks. How many parameters, in billions?
questions.why: 4,096² = 16,777,216. × 12 = 201 million per block. × 32 = 6.44 billion. (Llama 3 8B lands at 8.0B because of a gated MLP, shared key/value heads, and its large word tables.)

questions.prompt: Those 6.44 billion parameters stored at 16-bit (2 bytes each). How many GB?
questions.why: 6.44 billion × 2 bytes ≈ 12.9 GB. Rule of thumb: 16-bit weights take 2 GB per billion parameters.

questions.prompt: Why stack 32 blocks instead of one very wide block?
options: Depth chains steps: a later block uses an earlier block's note (“it's a riverside”) to add one (“floods likely”)
All 32 blocks share one set of weights, so depth adds reasoning steps without adding any parameters
Each block handles a different slice of the vocabulary, so 32 blocks cover more tokens than one wide block could
Stacking shrinks the KV cache, because only the last block keeps keys and values for earlier tokens
questions.why: One block is one round of talk-then-think. The blocks share a shape but each has its own weights, so depth costs memory, and a deeper model has a bigger KV cache (one entry per layer).

questions.prompt: How does the final vector for the last token become a probability for every token in the vocabulary?
options: The nearest row in the embedding table is found and that token gets probability 1, the rest 0
A dot product with each unembedding row gives one logit per token; softmax turns logits into probabilities
The last MLP outputs one probability per token directly, already summing to 1 across the whole vocabulary
Attention runs over the whole vocabulary, and each token's attention share is its probability
questions.why: logits = W_unembed · x: about 100,000 scores, one per vocabulary token, then softmax. The unembedding table has the same shape as the embedding table; some models share the two.

questions.prompt: The unembedding table is 100,000 × 4,096. About how many multiply-adds does scoring the vocabulary cost per generated token, in millions?
questions.why: One dot product of width 4,096 per vocabulary token: 100,000 × 4,096 = 409.6 million, for this step alone.

questions.prompt: What does temperature do, mechanically?
options: Adds random noise of size T to the weights, so each run of the same prompt differs a little
Divides the logits by T before softmax: small T stretches the gaps, large T shrinks them
Keeps only the top T tokens and renormalizes, so T = 1 always picks the single best token
Multiplies the logits by T after softmax, so a large T makes the top token even more likely
questions.why: p = softmax(logits / T). Dividing by a small number stretches the gaps, and softmax's exponent turns stretched gaps into a near-certain winner.

questions.prompt: Two candidate tokens with logits [2, 1]. At temperature T = 0.5, what probability does the first get, in percent?
questions.why: Divide by 0.5: [4, 2]. Softmax depends on the gap, 2: e² ÷ (e² + 1) ≈ 7.389 ÷ 8.389 ≈ 88%. At T = 1 it would be e ÷ (e + 1) ≈ 73%.

questions.prompt: As temperature approaches 0, what happens?
options: Greedy decoding: the top-scoring token is picked every time, so output repeats
Every token becomes equally likely, since dividing by a tiny T flattens all the gaps
The model stops generating, because no token keeps a nonzero probability
Answers become factually correct, since only the model's surest token survives
questions.why: The gaps grow without bound, so the top logit takes ~100% of the probability. Deterministic is not the same as correct: the top token can still be wrong.

questions.prompt: Top-p with p = 0.9. Sorted probabilities: 0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05. How many tokens are kept?
questions.why: Keep the smallest set that reaches p: 0.50 + 0.30 = 0.80 (not enough), + 0.15 = 0.95 ≥ 0.9. Three tokens; the 0.05 tail is cut.

questions.prompt: Same top-p cut (kept 0.50, 0.30, 0.15). After rescaling to 100%, what is the top token's probability, in percent?
questions.why: The kept tokens sum to 0.95, so each is divided by 0.95: 0.50 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 52.6%.

questions.prompt: Why use top-p instead of sampling from the full distribution?
options: It makes generation faster, since softmax only has to run over the few tokens that survive the cut
It cuts the long tail, so one unlucky draw can't derail a long answer, yet keeps variety among plausible tokens
It guarantees the same output every time, because the cut removes all randomness from sampling
It shrinks the KV cache, since tokens cut from the tail never need their keys and values stored on the GPU
questions.why: A long answer is hundreds of draws; thousands of tiny-probability tokens add up to a real chance of a bad pick somewhere. Top-p adapts the cut: few tokens when the model is sure, more when it isn't (top-k keeps a fixed k).

questions.prompt: Why are earlier tokens' keys and values still valid on the next generation pass?
options: A token only looks backward, so appending a token can't change what was computed for earlier ones
The model is quickly retrained after each token, so the stored keys and values are refreshed
Keys and values are random projections, so any stored value works as well as a fresh one
They aren't valid: every pass recomputes them, since each new token changes earlier tokens' context
questions.why: Position i only attends to positions 1…i. Adding position i+1 changes nothing about earlier positions, so their keys and values can be stored and reused.

questions.prompt: Without a cache, generating n tokens after a prompt costs about n × prompt + n²/2 token positions. Prompt 100, output 2,000. How many positions, in millions?
What exactly does the KV cache store?
options: The final output tokens of earlier requests, to answer repeated prompts
Every earlier token's key and value vectors, for every layer
The query vectors of every earlier token, in every layer
A copy of the model's weights in faster on-chip memory
questions.why: Keys and values are what a token offers to later tokens. Queries are only needed for the newest token, so they aren't kept. The cache grows by one entry per token per layer and lives in GPU memory for the whole request.

questions.prompt: With a KV cache, what does each decode step compute?
options: q, k and v for every token so far, then attend over all of them as on the first pass
q, k and v for the new token only; append its k and v to the cache; attend over the whole cache
Only the logits for the new token, since attention was already done for the cached tokens
k and v for every token again, but q only for the new token, then attend over the fresh k and v
questions.why: The new token still attends to everything before it, but reads stored keys and values instead of recomputing them.

questions.prompt: Which backend pattern is the KV cache most like?
options: Memoization: compute once, store, reuse because the inputs can't change
A message queue: each token's keys and values wait until the next pass consumes them
A write-ahead log used for crash recovery
Sharding: each layer's keys and values live on a different machine
questions.why: Earlier tokens' keys and values are pure functions of tokens that never change, so caching them is always safe: no invalidation needed within a request.

questions.prompt: Prefill vs decode: which sets which latency?
options: Prefill sets time to first token (TTFT); decode sets time per output token (TPOT)
Prefill sets time per output token (TPOT); decode sets time to first token (TTFT)
Both set TTFT; TPOT is fixed by the model size alone
Neither: network latency dominates both TTFT and TPOT
questions.why: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass and fills the cache before the first token can appear. Decode then produces tokens one tick at a time.

questions.prompt: Why is prefill compute-bound while single-user decode is memory-bound?
options: Prefill reuses each weight it reads across every prompt token; decode reads all weights for one token per user
Prefill runs on the CPU while decode runs on the GPU, whose memory is slower to reach than the CPU's
Decode does more math per token than prefill, because each output token must attend to the whole prompt again
Prefill skips attention and only runs the MLPs, so it has less memory to read per token than decode
questions.why: Same weights, different math per byte. Prefill does many tokens' worth of math per weight read; decode does one. Batching many users' decode ticks shares each weight read, which is why batching decides throughput.

questions.prompt: What does continuous batching change?
options: Requests join and leave the batch at every decode tick, rather than waiting for the batch to finish
All requests in a batch are padded to the same length, so the short ones finish with the longest one
The batch size is fixed at server start and every slot is kept busy by queuing requests
Prefill and decode run on separate models, so new prompts no longer pause the decode loop
questions.why: Scheduling per tick means a finished request frees its slot immediately and a new one starts without waiting for the longest answer in the batch.

questions.prompt: KV cache bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes per number. 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128, 16-bit. How many KB per token?
questions.why: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes ≈ 328 KB (320 KiB) per token. The 2 at the front is one key plus one value.

questions.prompt: Same model (327,680 bytes per token). How many GB for one 8,192-token request?
A 70B model at 16-bit (140 GB of weights) on two 80 GB GPUs. Ignoring every other overhead, how many 8K-token requests (2.68 GB of KV cache each) fit in the memory left over?
questions.why: 160 − 140 = 20 GB left. 20 ÷ 2.68 ≈ 7.5, so 7 whole requests, fewer once real overheads are counted. Concurrency is set by KV memory, not by compute.

questions.prompt: Which changes let more concurrent requests fit on the same GPUs? Pick all that apply.
options: Grouped-query attention (fewer KV heads)
Storing the KV cache at 8-bit instead of 16-bit
Quantizing the weights, freeing memory for caches
Raising the temperature
Using top-p sampling
questions.why: Anything that shrinks bytes per token or frees memory raises concurrency. Temperature and top-p only change which token is drawn; they don't touch memory.

questions.prompt: A model has 64 query heads. With grouped-query attention, 8 KV heads serve them. How many times smaller is the KV cache than with one KV head per query head?
questions.why: The cache stores one key and one value per KV head. 64 → 8 KV heads cuts it by 64 ÷ 8 = 8×, while every query head still gets its own query.

questions.prompt: Why do context windows have a limit? Pick all that apply.
options: KV memory grows in line with the number of tokens
Prefill attention work grows with the square of the number of tokens
The model only learned positions up to its training length
The vocabulary runs out of token IDs
The tokenizer can only split a fixed number of words
questions.why: Memory, compute and training. Vocabulary size is unrelated: the same IDs repeat as often as needed.

questions.prompt: Every request to a chatbot starts with the same 2,000-token system prompt. How could the server avoid redoing that work?
options: Keep the KV cache computed for that prefix and reuse it for requests that start with identical tokens
Lower the temperature while the system prompt is processed, so the model reads it in fewer forward passes
Send the system prompt only once per day, since the model remembers it between requests
Compress the prompt with gzip before sending it, so the model has fewer tokens to process
questions.why: Keys and values for a prefix depend only on the prefix's tokens, so identical prefixes give identical KV. Lesson 3 calls this prompt caching.
